content: Laryngitis is a condition characterized by inflammation of the larynx, which leads to a hoarse voice or even complete loss of voice due to irritation of the vocal cords. If the condition lasts for only a few days, it is classified as acute laryngitis. However, if it persists for more than three weeks, it is considered chronic laryngitis. Historically, laryngitis has been recognized for centuries. In 1840, Dr. Jordan Roche Lynch, an English physician, documented a case study on the treatment of acute laryngitis. More recently, in 2005, Drs. Reveiz, Cardona, and Ospina demonstrated that antibiotics are not effective in treating laryngitis. Laryngitis can be classified based on the duration of symptoms. Acute laryngitis typically has a sudden onset and resolves on its own within 3 to 5 days. Chronic laryngitis, on the other hand, lasts longer than three weeks. The larynx, or voice box, is located at the top of the trachea, which leads to the lungs. It houses the vocal cords. When the vocal cords become inflamed or infected, they swell, leading to hoarseness. In severe cases, this swelling can partially obstruct the airway. Laryngitis can result from both infectious and noninfectious causes. Viral infections are the most common cause and include viruses such as rhinovirus, adenovirus, influenza virus, parainfluenza virus, and respiratory syncytial virus. Bacterial causes, though less common, include pathogens like Staphylococcus aureus and Haemophilus influenzae. It is important to differentiate laryngitis from other conditions that may affect the larynx, such as upper respiratory tract infections, vocal fold cysts, nodules, polyps, or laryngeal stenosis. Acute laryngitis is more commonly seen in children, and women are more frequently affected than men. The incidence of laryngitis is higher in the winter months, with rates doubling compared to the summer. Routine screening for laryngitis is not recommended. In most cases, acute laryngitis resolves naturally within 3 to 7 days without treatment. Complications are generally mild and may include throat pain. The prognosis for laryngitis is excellent, with no associated mortality. The symptoms of laryngitis include hoarseness, coughing, and swollen lymph nodes. On physical examination, patients with laryngitis typically appear well. However, findings may include vocal fold cysts, nodules, or swollen lymph nodes in the neck. There are no specific laboratory tests or diagnostic findings associated with laryngitis. Imaging studies, such as X-rays, CT scans, or MRIs, are not typically useful in diagnosing laryngitis unless there is suspicion of pathology outside the larynx. Laryngoscopy is recommended if hoarseness persists for more than two weeks without an obvious benign cause. Treatment for viral laryngitis is primarily supportive, as there is no specific antiviral therapy. For infectious laryngitis caused by bacteria, antimicrobial therapy may be used. In cases of laryngitis related to gastroesophageal reflux, acid suppression therapy with medications like omeprazole or ranitidine is recommended. Surgery is not a first-line treatment for laryngitis and is generally reserved for cases involving persistent vocal cord nodules. Primary prevention strategies for laryngitis include avoiding contact with individuals who have upper respiratory infections, practicing good hand hygiene, and refraining from smoking.
